bands.label: Pre-K to kindergarten, about 4 and 5 years

grades.tested: A practice close to this one was tested in a study or rated in an evidence guide for children near this age.
grades.adapted: Supported by research on a different age or setting, or by correlational studies. The home routine itself is untested.
grades.plausible: Reasonable and low risk, but no reviewed study supports it directly.

activities.title: Read a decodable book aloud
activities.goal: Accurate, increasingly fluent decoding of connected text.
activities.do: The child reads a short book aloud that uses letter-sound patterns they have been taught. When they get stuck, prompt them to look at the letters and blend the sounds, not to guess from the picture. Reread the same book the next day for smoothness.
activities.easier: You read a page first, then the child reads the same page back.
activities.harder: A new book read cold; books with two-syllable words and new vowel patterns; reread a page to beat yesterday's smoothness.
activities.materials: A decodable book series matched to the patterns the child knows.
activities.why: Daily reading of connected text and decoding by sounding out are the two rated recommendations for beginning readers; each word decoded is a learning trial.
activities.notice: Does the child sound out or guess? Which patterns cause stops? Do rereads get smoother?

activities.title: Read aloud well above their own level
activities.goal: Vocabulary, knowledge of the world and listening comprehension.
activities.do: Read a picture book or chapter book that is far harder than anything the child could decode. Stop two or three times to ask an open question ("Why did she do that?", "What do you think happens next?") and explain two new words in plain language.
activities.easier: Shorter picture books; let the child choose; ask about the pictures.
activities.harder: Chapter books with few pictures; before reading, the child retells yesterday's chapter; nonfiction on a topic they care about.
activities.materials: Library books. A mix of stories and nonfiction.
activities.why: Storybook exposure feeds vocabulary and comprehension, a separate path from decoding (`senechal-2002`). Trained shared-reading programs have only a small effect on language, near zero against active comparison activities (`noble-2019`), so the case rests on daily volume and enjoyment more than on technique.
activities.notice: Which new words reappear in the child's own talk? Can they retell the story in order?

activities.title: Build and change words with letter tiles
activities.goal: Mapping sounds to spellings in both directions.
activities.do: Say a word and have the child build it with letter tiles. Then change one sound at a time: cat, cot, cop, chop, shop. The child says each new word after building it.
activities.easier: Three-sound words with short vowels, changing only the first sound.
activities.harder: Blends and digraphs (st, ch, sh), silent e (cap to cape), vowel teams, or building a word you only say aloud once.
activities.materials: Magnetic letters or letter tiles.
activities.why: Teaching letter-sound links and word analysis has strong evidence, and spelling a word draws on the same knowledge as reading it.
activities.notice: Which sound positions are hard: first, last or middle? Which patterns are not yet secure?

activities.title: Play with the sounds in words, no letters
activities.goal: Phonemic awareness: hearing and moving individual sounds.
activities.do: In the car or at the table, play quick sound games. Blend: "What word is /s/ /u/ /n/?" Segment: "What sounds are in 'ship'?" Delete: "Say 'smile' without the /s/."
activities.easier: Blend two parts (sun-shine), then first sound plus the rest (/m/ - /ap/).
activities.harder: Delete or swap a middle sound ("change the /i/ in 'ship' to /o/").
activities.materials: None.
activities.why: Phonological awareness is among the strongest preschool predictors of reading, and teaching it has strong evidence. Once a child decodes well, the harder manipulations are the useful ones.
activities.notice: Can the child do it without seeing letters? Which manipulation is the edge of their ability?

activities.title: Retell and explain a story
activities.goal: Narrative language and inference.
activities.do: After a book or a show, ask the child to tell what happened at the beginning, the middle and the end. Then ask one "why" question about a character's choice.
activities.easier: Retell with the book open, using the pictures.
activities.harder: Retell to someone who did not hear the story; change the ending; compare two books.
activities.materials: Any story.
activities.why: Building academic and narrative language is recommended, with minimal direct evidence for any one routine.
activities.notice: Does the retell keep order and cause? Does the child use words from the book?

activities.title: Hold a long back-and-forth conversation
activities.goal: Oral language through extended turn-taking.
activities.do: Once a day, follow the child's topic for at least five back-and-forth turns. Ask a real question, wait, then build on what they said. Add one precise word they did not use.
activities.easier: Talk about something in front of you both while doing it together.
activities.harder: Talk about something not present: yesterday, tomorrow's plan, how something works, a disagreement.
activities.materials: None. Meals, car rides and bedtime work well.
activities.why: Conversational turns, not the amount of adult talk, are what relate to language outcomes at 4-6. The evidence is correlational.
activities.notice: How many turns before the topic drops? Does the child ask you questions back?

activities.title: Write real messages, spelling by sound
activities.goal: Encoding sounds into letters for a real purpose.
activities.do: Give the child a real reason to write: a label, a shopping-list item, a note to a sibling, a sign for a fort. They say the word slowly and write the sounds they hear. Accept the attempt as written. Afterwards you may show the conventional spelling of one word.
activities.easier: You say the word slowly, stretching each sound; the child writes only the first and last sounds.
activities.harder: A whole sentence with spaces; rereading it tomorrow; fixing one word using a pattern they know.
activities.materials: Paper, sticky notes, fat pencil or marker.
activities.why: In a randomised trial, kindergartners with weak sound awareness who practised spelling by sound, with feedback, learned to read more words than those given sound-segmentation training or storybooks (`senechal-2012`). Invented-spelling skill also predicts later reading and spelling (`ouellette-2017`).
activities.notice: How many sounds per word does the child represent? Are vowels appearing?

activities.title: Practise forming letters correctly
activities.goal: Legible, automatic letter formation so handwriting stops limiting writing.
activities.do: Teach a few letters at a time with a consistent starting point and stroke order, saying the strokes aloud ("start at the top, big line down"). The child writes each letter five times and circles their best one. Start with the letters in their name.
activities.easier: Large letters on a whiteboard or in a tray of salt; trace, then copy.
activities.harder: Lowercase on lined paper; writing letters from memory when you say the sound; short words.
activities.materials: Whiteboard, or paper with a wide rule; short pencil or crayon.
activities.why: Explicit handwriting teaching improves legibility, fluency and the quality of writing from kindergarten up. Starting slightly earlier is an extrapolation.
activities.notice: Grip, where each letter starts, reversals, and whether the hand tires quickly.

activities.title: Dictate a story, then add your own words
activities.goal: Composing ideas separately from the mechanics of writing.
activities.do: The child tells a story or describes a drawing while you write it down exactly as said. Read it back, pointing to the words. The child writes the title, their name and any words they can.
activities.easier: One sentence about a drawing.
activities.harder: The child writes the first sentence and dictates the rest; a story with a problem and a solution; a second draft that adds one detail.
activities.materials: Paper and pencil. Staple pages into a book.
activities.why: Regular writing and learning the writing process are recommended for elementary students. Dictation lets a young child compose beyond what their hand allows.
activities.notice: Does the story have a sequence? Does the child notice when you read back something that does not sound right?

activities.title: Hand-strength and control work
activities.goal: Hand strength and precision for pencil, scissors and tools.
activities.do: Offer one precise hand task: cut along a drawn line, move small items with tongs or tweezers, roll and pinch clay, lace, thread beads, or copy a simple design with a pencil.
activities.easier: Snip strips of paper; large tongs; soft dough.
activities.harder: Cut curves and zigzags; copy a design from a card; draw a person with six or more parts.
activities.materials: Child scissors, tongs, clay or dough, beads and lace.
activities.why: Fine motor skill at school entry predicts later achievement, but no reviewed study shows that training it raises achievement. The direct value is easier writing and self-care.
activities.notice: Which hand does the child prefer? Is the helper hand holding the paper?
activities.safety: Small parts are a choking hazard for younger siblings. Supervise scissors.

activities.title: Sign and label your own things
activities.goal: Name writing and the idea that writing carries meaning.
activities.do: The child writes their name on every drawing and piece of work, and makes labels for their shelf, their seat or their creations.
activities.easier: First letter only, then first name with a model to copy.
activities.harder: First and last name from memory; a caption for a drawing; a card for someone.
activities.materials: Whatever is at hand.
activities.why: Name writing is the most advanced early writing skill at every preschool age and is one of the predictors of later literacy.
activities.notice: Letter order, letter size, and whether it is written from memory.

activities.title: Play a numbered board game, counting on
activities.goal: A mental number line: numbers as positions with size and order.
activities.do: Play a board game with numbered squares in a line. The child spins or rolls and says the number of each square as they move, counting on from where they are ("5, 6, 7"), not "1, 2" from the start of each move.
activities.easier: A 1-10 board with a 1-2 spinner.
activities.harder: A 1-100 board in rows of ten; "how many more to reach 20?"; two dice added together; moving backwards.
activities.materials: A linear numbered board (home-made is fine), spinner or die, tokens.
activities.why: The most directly tested home-style math activity for this age: about an hour of play in total produced gains on four number tasks that lasted at least nine weeks.
activities.notice: Does the child count on or restart from one? Can they say which of two numbers is bigger?

activities.title: Count real things and say how many
activities.goal: One-to-one counting, the last number as the total, and comparing amounts.
activities.do: Count real sets through the day: stairs, grapes, forks for the table. Ask "How many?" after counting, then "Get me 7." Compare two sets: which has more, and how many more?
activities.easier: Sets up to 5; touch each item as it is counted.
activities.harder: Sets to 20 and beyond; count on from a given number; count by tens; "how many would there be with two more?"
activities.materials: Household objects.
activities.why: Number and operations taught along a progression is the one early-math recommendation with more than minimal evidence. School-entry number skill is the strongest predictor of later achievement.
activities.notice: Does the child give the last number as the answer to "how many"? Where does the count sequence break?

activities.title: See how many without counting
activities.goal: Instant recognition of small quantities and of numbers as parts.
activities.do: Flash a dot card, a domino or some fingers for two seconds and ask how many. Then ask how they saw it ("I saw 3 and 2").
activities.easier: One to four dots in dice patterns.
activities.harder: Five to ten dots in two groups; ten-frames; "how many more to make 10?"
activities.materials: Dot cards, dice, dominoes.
activities.why: Recognising small quantities and seeing parts inside a whole are early steps in the reviewed number progression. This specific card routine is an adaptation.
activities.notice: Does the child know 5 as 4 and 1 or 3 and 2 without counting each dot?

activities.title: Solve a story problem from today
activities.goal: Addition and subtraction as stories about real things.
activities.do: At bedtime or a meal, pose one short problem from the child's day: "You had 4 crackers and ate 1. How many are left?" Let them use fingers or objects, then ask how they worked it out.
activities.easier: Totals to 5 with objects in hand.
activities.harder: Totals to 20; a missing part ("You have 3 and want 7. How many more?"); equal sharing between people.
activities.materials: None, or small objects.
activities.why: A year of short shared story problems raised first-graders' math achievement. Using them a year or two earlier is an extrapolation.
activities.notice: What strategy does the child use: counting all, counting on, or a known fact?

activities.title: Measure and compare
activities.goal: Length, weight and capacity as things you can compare and count.
activities.do: Compare two objects directly (longer, heavier, holds more), then measure with a repeated unit such as blocks or footsteps, and say the result as a number of units.
activities.easier: Line up three objects from shortest to longest.
activities.harder: A ruler or kitchen scale; estimate first, then measure; record results in a simple chart.
activities.materials: Blocks, string, measuring cups, kitchen scale.
activities.why: Measurement is part of the recommended early-math content, though the evidence for teaching it is rated minimal.
activities.notice: Does the child line up the ends? Do they leave gaps between units?

activities.title: Copy, extend and invent patterns
activities.goal: Seeing and describing a repeating unit.
activities.do: Make a repeating pattern with objects, claps or movements. The child copies it, extends it, and says what the repeating part is. Then they make one for you.
activities.easier: ABAB with two colours.
activities.harder: AAB, ABC and ABB patterns; translate a colour pattern into claps; find the mistake in your pattern; growing patterns (1, 2, 3 blocks).
activities.materials: Blocks, beads, cutlery, or the body.
activities.why: Patterns are part of the recommended early-math content, though the evidence for teaching them is rated minimal.
activities.notice: Can the child name the repeating unit, or only continue by eye?

activities.title: Predict, test, explain
activities.goal: Making a prediction, testing it, and revising an idea from evidence.
activities.do: Pick a question you can test in five minutes: what sinks, which ramp is faster, what a magnet picks up, what melts first. The child says what they think will happen and why, then tests it, then says what they saw. If they were wrong, ask what they think now.
activities.easier: A yes/no prediction on one object.
activities.harder: Change only one thing between two tries and say why that makes the test fair; draw the result.
activities.materials: Water tub, ramp and balls, magnet, ice, kitchen items.
activities.why: Preschoolers already reason from evidence, and guided play with an adult's questions beats both free play and plain telling for some outcomes. Unguided discovery alone does worse.
activities.notice: Does the child change their idea when the result disagrees with it?
activities.safety: Supervise water. Keep small magnets away from young children; swallowed magnets are dangerous.

activities.title: Explore a new thing before being shown
activities.goal: Self-directed exploration and discovery.
activities.do: When you hand over a new toy, tool or gadget, do not demonstrate it. Say "I wonder what this does" and wait. After a few minutes, ask what they found and what else it might do.
activities.easier: Explore it alongside them, narrating what you notice.
activities.harder: The child shows a sibling or parent what it does and how they found out.
activities.materials: Any unfamiliar, safe object with more than one function.
activities.why: Direct demonstration of one function made preschoolers explore less and discover fewer other functions. This is a lab finding for one session; it argues for holding back at first, not for never teaching.
activities.notice: How long does the child persist before asking for help? How many functions do they find?
activities.safety: Check the object for small parts, batteries and pinch points first.

activities.title: Turn a 'why' into 'how could we find out'
activities.goal: Explanations, and the habit of checking them.
activities.do: When the child asks why, give a real, short explanation. Then, once a day, add: "How could we find out?" and do it: look closely, try it, or look it up together.
activities.easier: Just answer the question properly instead of deflecting it.
activities.harder: The child proposes the test, or explains the answer to someone else the next day.
activities.materials: A magnifier and library nonfiction help.
activities.why: Preschoolers' questions are a real learning mechanism: they ask a great many, and persist until they get an informative answer.
activities.notice: Are the questions shifting from 'what' to 'why' and 'how'?

activities.title: Watch one thing change and record it
activities.goal: Careful observation over time.
activities.do: Choose something that changes over days: a seed, the moon, a puddle, the weather, a caterpillar. Look at the same time each day and have the child draw or mark what they see.
activities.easier: A weather chart with stickers.
activities.harder: Measure and record a number each day; predict tomorrow's; explain the pattern at the end of the week.
activities.materials: Notebook, pencil, ruler.
activities.cadence: daily for a week or two
activities.why: No reviewed study tests this routine. It is a low-cost way to practise looking closely and linking drawing, counting and talk.
activities.notice: Does the drawing show what is there, or what the child expects to be there?

activities.title: Throw and catch, taught properly
activities.goal: Object-control skills that team sports depend on.
activities.do: Practise in short sets. Catching: start with a large soft ball from close range, hands ready, eyes on the ball. Throwing overhand: side on to the target, step with the opposite foot, follow through. Give one cue at a time and ten tries.
activities.easier: Roll and trap; catch a balloon or a scarf; underhand toss into a bucket.
activities.harder: A tennis ball; a longer distance; a moving target; catching on the run; throwing with the other hand.
activities.materials: Balls of several sizes, a bucket or wall target.
activities.why: Fundamental movement skills improve with instruction and practice and did not improve with free play alone. Children who have them stay more active.
activities.notice: Does the child step with the opposite foot? Do they trap the ball against the chest or catch with the hands?

activities.title: Kick, strike and dribble
activities.goal: The remaining object-control skills: kicking, striking, dribbling with feet and hands.
activities.do: Choose one skill per session. Kick a still ball at a target with the laces. Hit a ball off a tee or a cone. Dribble a soccer ball around cones, or bounce a basketball with one hand while walking.
activities.easier: A large still ball; a short fat bat; bounce and catch with two hands.
activities.harder: A rolling ball; a pitched ball; dribbling at a run or with the weaker foot or hand.
activities.materials: Soccer ball, tee and bat, bouncy ball, cones.
activities.why: Same evidence as throwing and catching: these skills respond to teaching and practice, not to free play alone.
activities.notice: Which side is weaker? Does the child watch the ball through contact?

activities.title: Hop, skip, jump and balance
activities.goal: Locomotor and balance skills.
activities.do: Set up a short course: hop on one foot, gallop, skip, jump for distance from two feet, walk a line or a low beam, land softly from a step. Time a lap and try to beat it.
activities.easier: Jump over a line; walk a wide line; gallop.
activities.harder: Skip smoothly; hop ten times on each foot; walk a beam backwards; jump rope.
activities.materials: Tape, a low beam or kerb, cones, a rope.
activities.why: Locomotor skills are part of the fundamental movement skills that respond to instruction.
activities.notice: Can the child skip yet? Is one leg clearly weaker for hopping?

activities.title: An hour of hard play every day
activities.goal: Enough daily moderate-to-vigorous activity.
activities.do: Make sure each day includes at least an hour of activity that leaves the child out of breath: chasing, biking, climbing, swimming, playground games. Count what happens at school and add the rest.
activities.easier: Three 20-minute bursts.
activities.harder: A long hike or bike ride; setting their own distance or time goal.
activities.materials: Outdoor space, a bike or scooter with helmet.
activities.why: This is the guideline floor for ages 3-4 and for ages 6 and up. The underlying evidence is rated low quality but the direction is consistent.
activities.notice: On which days of the week does this not happen?
activities.safety: Helmet for wheels. Sun and water safety.

activities.title: Learn to swim
activities.goal: Water competency: float, turn, reach the wall, and swim a short distance.
activities.do: Enrol in swim lessons and keep going until the child can enter deep water, surface, turn, float or tread, and swim to an exit. Practise between lessons at a pool.
activities.easier: Parent-and-child water play: blowing bubbles, floating with support, jumping in to you.
activities.harder: Swim a width unaided; retrieve an object from the bottom; swim in clothes under supervision.
activities.materials: A pool and a qualified instructor.
activities.why: Formal lessons were associated with a large drop in drowning risk at ages 1-4, and paediatric guidance recommends them. Lessons are one layer of protection, never a replacement for supervision.
activities.notice: Can the child get back to the wall alone after jumping in?
activities.safety: Constant close adult supervision in and near water, whatever the child's skill.

activities.title: Play small-sided team games across several sports
activities.goal: Playing with others under simple rules, and sampling many sports.
activities.do: Join a low-key league or play pickup games with a few children: 3-a-side soccer, tee-ball, flag tag, basketball on a low hoop. Change sport by season. Afterwards, talk about effort and what was fun, not the score.
activities.easier: Parent-and-child games with one rule; skill stations before any game.
activities.harder: Positions and passing; keeping score and handling a loss; a second sport in the same year.
activities.materials: A local recreation league or a few friends and a ball.
activities.why: Paediatric guidance favours fun, skills and several sports over early competition and specialization. Many children under 6 are not yet ready for team tactics, so expect to coach skills more than strategy.
activities.notice: Does the child stay engaged when they do not have the ball? How do they take losing?

activities.title: Allow risky outdoor play
activities.goal: Judging risk, managing fear, and physical confidence.
activities.do: Let the child climb high, go fast, balance on things, wrestle and play slightly out of your sight, in a place you have checked for serious hazards. Step back. Ask "What is your plan?" in place of saying "Be careful."
activities.easier: Low climbing and jumping with you nearby.
activities.harder: A taller tree; a steeper hill on the bike; using a real tool such as a hammer or a peeler with instruction.
activities.materials: Playground, trees, hills, loose logs, a bike.
activities.why: Risky outdoor play is associated with more physical activity and better social health, with no increase in fractures from play at height. The evidence is observational.
activities.notice: Does the child assess before acting? Do they stop themselves at their own limit?
activities.safety: Remove hazards the child cannot see or judge (traffic, deep water, hard falls onto concrete). Risk the child can see and choose is the point.

activities.title: Do not take over a hard task
activities.goal: Persistence on something difficult but doable.
activities.do: When the child is stuck on a puzzle, a zip, a word or a build, wait at least ten seconds. Then give the smallest hint that helps ("What have you tried?", "Look at this corner"). Do not do it for them. If you must help, teach the step and hand it back.
activities.easier: Do the first step together, then stop.
activities.harder: A harder task chosen on purpose; the child states what they will try next before you say anything.
activities.materials: Any task at the edge of the child's ability.
activities.why: Four- and five-year-olds persisted less after an adult took over a hard task than after an adult taught or did nothing (`leonard-2021`). Parents who kept directing an already engaged kindergartner had children with poorer self-regulation (`obradovic-2021`), and overcontrol at 2 predicted poorer regulation at 5 (`perry-2018`); those two are correlational.
activities.notice: How long does the child try before asking for help? Does that time grow?

activities.title: Name the effort and the strategy
activities.goal: Linking results to what the child did.
activities.do: When the child succeeds or keeps trying, say specifically what they did: "You tried three ways to make it balance", "You sounded out every letter". Skip "You're so smart."
activities.easier: One specific comment a day.
activities.harder: Ask the child what they did that worked, so they say it themselves.
activities.materials: None.
activities.why: Praise for intelligence led older children to persist less after failure than praise for effort (`mueller-dweck-1998`), but replications have failed (`li-bates-2019`) and mindset effects on achievement are very small (`sisk-2018`). Inflated praise backfired for children with low self-esteem (`brummelman-2014`). Treat specific, accurate praise as a cheap habit, not a lever.
activities.notice: Does the child start describing their own strategies?

activities.title: Name feelings precisely
activities.goal: A vocabulary for emotions, in themselves and in others.
activities.do: Name feelings in the moment and in books using precise words: frustrated, disappointed, nervous, proud, jealous. Ask what a character feels and how you can tell. After a hard moment has passed, talk through what the feeling was and what helped.
activities.easier: Happy, sad, mad, scared, with faces.
activities.harder: Two feelings at once; what someone else felt in a conflict; what they could do next time.
activities.materials: Picture books help.
activities.why: Emotion knowledge and regulation at 3-4 predict social competence in kindergarten. The evidence is correlational.
activities.notice: Does the child use a feeling word in place of acting the feeling out?

activities.title: Play games that require stopping and waiting
activities.goal: Inhibition, working memory, turn-taking and losing well.
activities.do: Play games where the child must hold back or remember a rule: Simon Says, Red Light Green Light, freeze dance, and simple board and card games with turns and a winner.
activities.easier: Freeze dance; cooperative games.
activities.harder: Reverse the rule (move on "red", touch your toes when told "touch your head"); games with strategy; longer games they might lose.
activities.materials: A few simple board and card games.
activities.why: Activities that keep raising the demand on executive function can improve it, with narrow transfer. These particular games are a common adaptation, not a tested program.
activities.notice: Can the child hold the rule when excited? How do they react to losing?

activities.title: One small brave thing
activities.goal: Approaching something uncomfortable in small, chosen steps.
activities.do: With the child, pick one slightly scary thing to do this week: order their own food, say hello to a new child, ask a shop assistant a question, try a new food, go down the big slide. Agree the step beforehand, let them do it, and afterwards talk about how it felt before and after.
activities.easier: You do it together, or the child does only the first part.
activities.harder: The child chooses the challenge; the next step up the same ladder the week after.
activities.materials: None.
activities.why: Teaching parents of very shy preschoolers to reduce overprotection and encourage gradual steps toward feared situations cut later anxiety diagnoses (`rapee-2005`), and a parent-only program that reduced accommodation of anxiety matched therapy for older children (`lebowitz-2020`). Both are trials in children selected for shyness or anxiety; the weekly routine for a typical child is an adaptation.
activities.notice: Does the before-and-after gap in fear shrink over repeats?
activities.safety: The child chooses and can decline. Do not force. Persistent, impairing fear is a question for the child's clinician.

activities.title: Plan it, do it, review it
activities.goal: Planning ahead and reflecting afterwards.
activities.do: Before play or a project, ask "What is your plan?" and have the child say or draw it. Afterwards ask what happened, what changed, and what they would do next time.
activities.easier: Choose between two plans you offer.
activities.harder: A plan with three steps; a plan that needs materials gathered first; a plan made with a sibling.
activities.materials: Paper and pencil, optionally.
activities.why: Planning and reviewing play is a core routine in preschool curricula that were reviewed for executive function, with mixed later results.
activities.notice: Does the child stick to the plan or notice when they change it?

activities.title: Own one real household job
activities.goal: Responsibility for a job that matters to the family.
activities.do: Give the child one real, recurring job that they own from start to finish: setting the table, feeding a pet, emptying the small bins, watering plants. Teach it once, step by step, then expect it daily without doing it for them.
activities.easier: A job done alongside you.
activities.harder: A second job; a job with several steps (unload the cutlery and put it away); noticing it needs doing without a reminder.
activities.materials: Whatever the job needs, stored where the child can reach it.
activities.why: Chores in kindergarten are associated with later self-competence (`white-2019`), but not all studies agree. In experiments, asking children to 'be a helper' raised helping (`bryan-2014`) but made them give up more after a setback (`foster-hanson-2020`), and material rewards reduced toddlers' later helping (`warneken-2008`). So ask them to help, do not pay with things, and expect the job daily.
activities.notice: How many reminders does it take? Does the child check their own work?

activities.title: Get ready without help
activities.goal: Dressing, fastening and packing independently.
activities.do: Teach the fastenings one at a time: zip, buttons, shoes on the right feet, then laces. Put a picture checklist by the door for the morning routine and let the child run it. Leave enough time that you are not tempted to step in.
activities.easier: You start the zip; slip-on shoes.
activities.harder: Laces; packing their own bag from a list; choosing clothes for the weather.
activities.materials: A picture checklist; clothes the child can manage.
activities.why: No reviewed study isolates self-care routines. The case rests on autonomy support and on the practical value of the skills.
activities.notice: Which step still needs you? Is the limit skill or time?

activities.title: Pour, carry and clean up
activities.goal: Controlled, careful movement with real consequences.
activities.do: Let the child pour their own drink from a small jug, carry their plate to the sink, wipe a spill, sweep crumbs into a dustpan and put their own things away.
activities.easier: A half-full small jug; a damp cloth for the table.
activities.harder: Pour for the family; load the dishwasher; fold and put away their own laundry.
activities.materials: Small jug, cloth, child-size broom and dustpan.
activities.why: Practical-life work is one part of a Montessori program that did well in a lottery study. The study cannot attribute the result to this part.
activities.notice: Does the child notice and fix their own spill?

activities.title: Run an errand alone
activities.goal: Remembering and carrying out a multi-step task without an adult beside them.
activities.do: Send the child on a real errand with two or three steps: "Get the blue towel from the bathroom, put it by the door, then tell Dad it's there." In shops and restaurants, have them order, pay or ask for something themselves.
activities.easier: A one-step errand in the next room.
activities.harder: Four steps; an errand to a neighbour; buying one item while you wait nearby.
activities.materials: None.
activities.why: No reviewed study tests this. It loads working memory and gives practice at acting without an adult.
activities.notice: How many steps can the child hold? Do they come back to check or finish it?
activities.safety: Match the distance and setting to the child's road sense and your own judgement.

activities.title: Prepare part of the meal
activities.goal: Real food skills and willingness to eat what they made.
activities.do: Give the child a real part of dinner: wash vegetables, tear lettuce, snap beans, peel a carrot, cut soft foods with a child-safe knife. Serve what they made and say that they made it.
activities.easier: Washing and tearing.
activities.harder: Peeling; cutting firmer foods with a real small knife under close supervision; making a whole salad or snack plate.
activities.materials: Child-safe knife, peeler, board, a stable step.
activities.why: Children who helped cook ate more of the meal, salad especially, in one experiment with 6-10-year-olds. Evidence at this age is thin.
activities.notice: Does the child eat or at least taste what they prepared?
activities.safety: Close supervision with knives and peelers. Keep the child away from heat unless you are hands-on. Know the family's allergens.

activities.title: Follow a recipe and measure
activities.goal: Following steps in order; counting and measuring for a purpose.
activities.do: Choose a simple recipe with pictures. The child finds each ingredient, measures with cups and spoons, counts scoops aloud and does each step in order.
activities.easier: Three ingredients; you hold the cup while they scoop.
activities.harder: Read the numbers and words themselves; halve or double it with your help; "we need 1 cup and only have the half cup: how many?"
activities.materials: Measuring cups and spoons, a picture recipe.
activities.why: No reviewed study links cooking to math or reading. It is a natural setting for the counting and measuring in the math recommendations.
activities.notice: Does the child level the cup? Do they keep track of how many scoops?
activities.safety: Raw egg and flour are not for tasting. Adult handles the oven and hob.

activities.title: Crack, mix, spread and pour
activities.goal: Hand control with real kitchen tools.
activities.do: Teach one kitchen movement at a time: crack an egg into a separate bowl, whisk, stir a thick batter, spread with a butter knife, pour batter, roll dough.
activities.easier: Stirring and spreading.
activities.harder: Crack an egg with no shell in the bowl; flip a pancake with you at the hob; knead dough.
activities.materials: Bowls, whisk, butter knife, rolling pin.
activities.why: No reviewed evidence specific to cooking. It is purposeful fine and gross motor practice.
activities.notice: How much force and control does the child have with each tool?
activities.safety: Wash hands after raw egg. Adult controls anything hot.

activities.title: Taste and describe a new food
activities.goal: Willingness to try unfamiliar foods, and words for taste and texture.
activities.do: Pick one vegetable the child does not like. Offer a small taste of it every day for about two weeks, alongside familiar food. The child smells it, touches it, tastes it and describes it (crunchy, sour, bitter, soft). Do not pressure, bribe or ask them to finish it.
activities.easier: Smell and touch only.
activities.harder: Compare two varieties (two apples, two cheeses) and say which they prefer and why; choose a new vegetable at the shop to cook.
activities.materials: A small portion of one new food.
activities.cadence: daily for two weeks, then a new food
activities.why: In a randomised trial with children aged 2-6, a small daily taste of one vegetable for 14 days increased liking and intake of it, while nutrition information did nothing (`wardle-2003`). Pressure to eat reduced intake and caused negative comments (`galloway-2006`).
activities.notice: Does refusal soften over repeated offers?
activities.safety: Follow the family's allergy plan and cut foods to a safe size.

activities.title: Spend real time outdoors in daylight
activities.goal: Daily daylight and outdoor activity.
activities.do: Get outside in daylight every day, on top of whatever happens at school. Walk somewhere you would normally drive, eat outside, or move an indoor activity outdoors.
activities.easier: Twenty minutes after school.
activities.harder: Two hours or more on weekend days; outdoors in rain and cold with the right clothes.
activities.materials: Clothes for the weather.
activities.why: More time outdoors in daylight reduces the onset of short-sightedness in school-age children in trials (`he-2015`, `wu-2018`, `xiong-2017`). More outdoor time at daycare went with better working memory and attention from 4 to 7 (`ulset-2017`), a correlational finding.
activities.notice: On which days does this not happen, and why?
activities.safety: Sun protection, and clothing for cold and wet.

activities.title: Return to the same place and notice what changed
activities.goal: Close observation of living things and seasons.
activities.do: Choose one tree, pond, garden bed or stretch of path and visit it every week or two. Each time ask: what is different, what is the same, and what do you think will happen next? Collect one thing or take a photo.
activities.easier: A walk where the child finds three living things.
activities.harder: Keep a nature notebook with drawings and dates; learn the names of five local trees or birds.
activities.materials: A magnifier, a bag for finds, a notebook.
activities.why: Claims that nature time improves learning rest on weak evidence. This is included for observation skills and knowledge of the living world.
activities.notice: Does the child remember what it looked like last time?
activities.safety: Teach "look, don't eat" for berries and fungi. Check for ticks where relevant.

activities.title: Grow a plant or care for an animal
activities.goal: Sustained care for a living thing, and seeing a life cycle.
activities.do: Give the child charge of something alive: beans in a pot, a herb on the windowsill, a bird feeder, or a daily part of caring for a pet. They water or feed it on a schedule and tell you what they notice.
activities.easier: Water one plant with you.
activities.harder: Measure and chart growth; grow something to eat; work out why a plant is struggling.
activities.materials: Seeds, pot, soil, watering can; or pet-care supplies.
activities.why: No reviewed evidence of developmental benefit. One chore study found pet-care chores unrelated to executive function. Included for knowledge and responsibility.
activities.notice: Does the child remember without being asked?
activities.safety: Wash hands after soil and animals. Supervise all contact with animals.

activities.title: Free play in a natural space
activities.goal: Self-directed outdoor play with natural materials.
activities.do: Take the child to a wood, creek, beach or rough field and let them lead: digging, damming, stacking sticks, collecting, climbing. Bring nothing but a bucket and stay at a distance.
activities.easier: A park corner with sticks, leaves and mud.
activities.harder: Longer stretches; building a den or a dam with a friend or sibling.
activities.materials: Old clothes, boots, a bucket.
activities.why: Unstructured nature play is associated with more physical activity and better social and emotional outcomes. The evidence quality is rated low.
activities.notice: What does the child choose to do when nothing is suggested?
activities.safety: Constant close supervision near water. Check the area for serious hazards first.

activities.title: Study one animal in depth
activities.goal: Deep knowledge of one topic, built from books and from looking.
activities.do: Let the child choose one animal. Read two or three nonfiction books about it, watch it if you can (yard, zoo, video of real behaviour), and have the child draw it and tell someone three true things about it.
activities.easier: One picture book and a drawing.
activities.harder: Compare two animals; make a small book of facts; work out what it eats and what eats it.
activities.materials: Library nonfiction; a zoo, farm or backyard.
activities.why: No reviewed study tests topic studies at this age. Knowledge of the world supports later reading comprehension, and nonfiction read-alouds are one way to build it.
activities.notice: Which facts stick, and does the child link them to other animals?

activities.title: Build to match a model
activities.goal: Analysing a structure into parts and their positions.
activities.do: Build a small structure from blocks or bricks behind a screen, or use a picture or the instruction booklet. The child builds one that matches exactly, then checks it against yours.
activities.easier: Four or five blocks, with the model in view and built in front of them.
activities.harder: More pieces; a picture in place of a real model; a model seen for ten seconds then hidden; building the mirror image.
activities.materials: Unit blocks, interlocking bricks or magnetic tiles.
activities.why: A kindergarten block-building program, rated by the What Works Clearinghouse as a well-run randomised trial, improved spatial skills (`casey-2008`), and spatial training transfers to untrained spatial tasks (`uttal-2013`). Building from a model is related to early math (`verdine-2014`).
activities.notice: Does the child check the model piece by piece, or build from a general impression?
activities.safety: Small bricks are a choking hazard for younger siblings.

activities.title: Do harder and harder puzzles
activities.goal: Mental rotation and fitting parts into a whole.
activities.do: Keep jigsaws and shape puzzles available and move up in difficulty when one becomes easy. Talk about strategy: edges first, sort by colour, turn the piece.
activities.easier: 24 pieces with a clear picture.
activities.harder: 60-100 pieces; tangram or pattern-block pictures without internal lines; work without looking at the box.
activities.materials: Jigsaws, tangrams, pattern blocks.
activities.why: Puzzle play in the preschool years predicts later spatial skill, and spatial skills are trainable. The puzzle evidence is correlational.
activities.notice: Does the child rotate a piece in their head before trying it, or by trial and error?

activities.title: Use spatial words while building
activities.goal: Vocabulary for position, shape and movement.
activities.do: While the child builds, draws or tidies, use and ask for precise spatial words: above, below, between, behind, next to, edge, corner, side, rotate, flip, taller, wider, half. Give directions using them ("put the short one between the two tall ones").
activities.easier: In, on, under, next to.
activities.harder: Left and right; the child gives you building instructions without pointing.
activities.materials: None beyond the building materials.
activities.why: Parents' use of spatial words predicts children's use of them, which predicts later spatial skill. Guided play improves spatial vocabulary more than free play.
activities.notice: Which spatial words does the child now use unprompted?

activities.title: Build to solve a problem
activities.goal: Designing, testing, and improving after a failure.
activities.do: Set a challenge with a clear test: a bridge across a 30 cm gap that holds a toy car, the tallest tower that stands for ten seconds, a ramp that gets a ball into a cup, a boat that floats five coins. When it fails, ask what they will change.
activities.easier: The tallest tower they can make.
activities.harder: Limited materials; two constraints at once; draw the plan first; improve a design that already works.
activities.materials: Blocks, card, tape, tubes, recycling.
activities.why: No reviewed study tests design challenges at this age. The format follows guided play: the adult sets the goal and the child controls the solving.
activities.notice: How does the child respond to the first collapse?

activities.title: Make and use a simple map
activities.goal: Relating a small drawing to a real space.
activities.do: Draw a simple map of a room or the garden together, marking big landmarks. Hide something and mark it with an X for the child to find. Then they hide something and mark the map for you.
activities.easier: A map of one room with three landmarks, with you pointing to where you are standing.
activities.harder: The whole house or a park; turn the map so it does not line up with the room; the child draws the map.
activities.materials: Paper, pencil, something to hide.
activities.why: No reviewed study tests this routine. It practises matching a representation to a space, one of the spatial skills that training improves.
activities.notice: Does the child turn the map to match the room, or work it out without turning?

activities.title: Regular time with a fluent speaker
activities.goal: Real understanding and use of a second language.
activities.do: Arrange regular, sustained time with a person who speaks the language fluently and uses only that language with the child: a relative, a caregiver, a playgroup or an immersion class. Aim for hours each week across years, in real activities.
activities.easier: One recurring playdate or class a week.
activities.harder: An immersion school or program; a trip or stay where only that language is used.
activities.materials: A fluent speaker.
activities.cadence: several times a week, for years
activities.why: How well a language is learned depends on the amount and quality of live exposure. Starting before about 10 leaves native-like grammar within reach. Do this because the language matters to the family; a general cognitive benefit is not supported.
activities.notice: Does the child understand without translation? Do they answer in the language?

activities.title: Songs and routines in the language
activities.goal: Familiarity with the sounds and a small stock of words and phrases.
activities.do: Use the language for a few fixed routines: greetings, counting stairs, a mealtime phrase, three or four songs.
activities.easier: One song.
activities.harder: Simple questions and answers inside the routine.
activities.materials: Songs from a fluent source.
activities.why: This gives exposure and positive feeling toward the language. It will not produce proficiency on its own.
activities.notice: Does the child use any of the phrases unprompted?

activities.title: Shared books in the language
activities.goal: Vocabulary in context, with an adult.
activities.do: Read simple picture books in the language with the child, pointing and talking about the pictures in that language. An adult who speaks it should lead.
activities.easier: A book of single labelled pictures.
activities.harder: The child retells a page in the language.
activities.materials: Picture books in the language.
activities.why: No reviewed study tests this for second-language learners at this age. Infants learned a new language's sounds from a live person and not from recordings, so the adult matters more than the media.
activities.notice: Which words does the child recognise on a second reading?

activities.title: Make something with no model to copy
activities.goal: Choosing, planning and making for its own sake.
activities.do: Set out real materials and no example to copy. Let the child decide what to make. Describe what you see ("you used long blue lines here") in place of judging it, and ask them to tell you about it.
activities.easier: Two materials and a large sheet of paper.
activities.harder: Plan first ("what will you make, and what do you need?"); return to the same piece the next day; combine materials.
activities.materials: Paint, clay, collage scraps, glue, cardboard, tape.
activities.why: No study tests this routine. Drawing tends to decline with age, and the adults around a child shape whether it continues (`rose-2006`). Describing rather than gushing matters: inflated praise for a drawing led children with low self-esteem to avoid harder tasks (`brummelman-2014`).
activities.notice: Does the child plan, or discover as they go? How long do they stay with it?
activities.safety: Check that materials are non-toxic. Keep small collage pieces from younger siblings.

activities.title: Try a new medium each month
activities.goal: Breadth: meeting materials and techniques the child would not choose alone.
activities.do: Once a month, introduce one medium the child has not used: watercolour, clay, printmaking with cut vegetables, charcoal, weaving, photography with an old phone. Show the one technique it needs, then let them explore it over a few sessions.
activities.easier: One short session with you working alongside.
activities.harder: Make a finished piece in the new medium; combine it with a medium they already know; teach the technique to someone else.
activities.materials: Changes monthly; most cost little.
activities.why: No study tests rotating media. Interest begins as something triggered from outside and needs support before it becomes the child's own (`hidi-renninger-2006`), so the adult's job is to supply new triggers and notice which ones hold.
activities.notice: Which media does the child return to unprompted?
activities.safety: Ventilate for paints and glues; supervise any cutting tools.

activities.title: Draw something real by looking
activities.goal: Looking closely and translating what is seen into marks.
activities.do: Put one real object in front of the child (a shoe, a leaf, a toy animal). Ask what shapes they can see in it, then have them draw it while looking back at it often.
activities.easier: Trace around the object first, then add what is inside the outline.
activities.harder: Draw it again from another side; add shading or texture; draw a person who is sitting for them.
activities.materials: Paper, pencil, a real object.
activities.why: Drawing from observation draws on perception and memory (`fan-2023`) and practises pencil control. No study tests it for wider benefit at this age.
activities.notice: Does the child look back at the object while drawing?

activities.title: Draw it, then tell it
activities.goal: Recalling and organising an experience, and giving it a form.
activities.do: After an outing or event, the child draws what happened and then tells you about the drawing. Write one sentence of their words under it. Keep the drawings in a book they can look back at.
activities.easier: Draw one thing they saw.
activities.harder: Draw it as a sequence of three pictures; the child writes the caption by sound.
activities.materials: Paper or a sketchbook, pencils.
activities.why: Five- and six-year-olds who drew while describing an outing reported more correct information than those who only talked (`butler-1995`). One lab study; the home routine is an adaptation.
activities.notice: Does the drawing help the child tell more, or in better order?

activities.title: Cut, fold and build with paper and card
activities.goal: Tool control and turning flat material into a form.
activities.do: Give the child scissors, tape and card, and a goal they choose: a mask, a crown, a box, a paper aeroplane. Help only with steps they cannot physically do.
activities.easier: Cut and stick a collage.
activities.harder: Follow folding steps from pictures; make something that has to stand up or hold weight.
activities.materials: Card, paper, child scissors, tape, glue.
activities.why: No reviewed evidence beyond the general association between fine motor skill and later achievement. Overlaps with building.
activities.notice: How does the child solve the join or the fold when it fails the first time?

activities.title: Look at a picture and say what is going on
activities.goal: Describing, inferring and backing up an opinion.
activities.do: Look at one painting, photograph or illustration together. Ask "What is going on here?", then "What do you see that makes you say that?", then "What else can you find?"
activities.easier: Name things in the picture and their colours.
activities.harder: Compare two pictures of the same subject; guess what happened just before.
activities.materials: Art books, museum websites, or good picture-book illustrations.
activities.why: After a guided museum visit built around discussing real paintings, students wrote about an unfamiliar painting with more critical-thinking strategies (`bowen-2014`). That trial was with older children and included the visit itself.
activities.notice: Does the child point to evidence in the picture for what they say?

activities.title: Visit a gallery or museum with a plan
activities.goal: Seeing real art, and practice looking for longer than a glance.
activities.do: Once a month, visit a gallery, museum or public art. Pick three works only. At each one, use the look-and-talk questions, then let the child choose one to draw or act out at home.
activities.easier: Ten minutes, one room, one work the child picks.
activities.harder: The child plans the route from a map; compare two works by the same artist; tell a sibling about one piece.
activities.materials: A local art museum, many free; a sketchbook.
activities.why: A lottery-assigned museum visit improved critical thinking about art, most for younger and disadvantaged students (`bowen-2014`), and more school arts learning reduced discipline problems and raised writing and empathy (`bowen-2023`). Both concern school programs with older children.
activities.notice: Which works hold the child's attention, and what do they say about them a week later?
activities.safety: Keep hands off the art and stay together in crowds.

activities.title: Play drama games
activities.goal: Controlling emotions and the body on purpose, through pretending.
activities.do: Play short theatre games: freeze in a shape on a signal, walk like a character who is happy, then scared, then sneaky; show a feeling with only your face; pass an imaginary object round and change what it is. Take turns being the director.
activities.easier: Copy the adult's character before inventing one.
activities.harder: Switch emotions quickly on a cue; hold a character while someone tries to make them laugh; act a feeling and let others guess.
activities.materials: Space to move; a few props.
activities.why: In a randomised trial, eight weeks of dramatic pretend play games improved emotional self-control in 4- to 6-year-olds, while block play and storytime did not; there was no effect on empathy or social skills (`goldstein-2018`). That was a class with a teacher, so home doses are untested.
activities.notice: Can the child hold a character, or a freeze, when they want to laugh or move?

activities.title: Act out a story
activities.goal: Retelling a story in order, in voices and actions.
activities.do: After reading a book with a clear plot, act it out together with simple props. The child chooses a role, then swaps. Keep to the story's order of events.
activities.easier: Act out one scene.
activities.harder: Perform it for the family; change the ending and act the new version; make a puppet show of it.
activities.materials: A picture book with a clear plot; dress-up items or puppets.
activities.why: Classroom drama has been linked with story recall and oral language, with larger effects for enacting a set plot (`podlozny-2000`), but a review found the studies too flawed to rely on (`mages-2008`).
activities.notice: Does the child keep the events in order, and use the book's words?

activities.title: See live theatre or dance
activities.goal: Following a live story, and seeing other people's art made in front of them.
activities.do: Every month or two, see a live children's play, puppet show or dance performance. Afterwards, ask what happened, who they liked and why, and what they would change.
activities.easier: A 30-minute show; library or park performances.
activities.harder: Retell the plot in order; act out a favourite scene at home; see the book version and compare.
activities.materials: Local children's theatre, library and park programs.
activities.why: In five lottery experiments, school students who saw live theatre gained in tolerance, perspective taking and knowledge of the plot, while those who saw the film did not (`greene-2017`). School-age children; not tested at 4-6.
activities.notice: Can the child retell the plot? Do they talk about why characters acted as they did?

activities.title: Keep a steady beat and echo rhythms
activities.goal: Feeling and keeping a pulse; hearing and reproducing a pattern.
activities.do: Put on music with a clear beat and clap, march or drum along together. Then clap a short rhythm for the child to echo, and swap roles. Clap the syllables of names and words ("but-ter-fly", "wa-ter-mel-on").
activities.easier: Bounce or march to the beat while you hold their hands.
activities.harder: Keep the beat as the music speeds up or slows down; echo longer patterns; keep a beat while you clap a different rhythm.
activities.materials: Any music; a drum, pot or lap.
activities.why: In a small randomised trial, a preschool music program improved 5- and 6-year-olds' awareness of words and syllables as much as a phonological program (`dege-2011`), and beat-keeping goes with better neural encoding of speech (`woodruff-2014`). The home routine is an adaptation; do it first for the musical skill.
activities.notice: Can the child stay with the beat, or do they drift ahead?

activities.title: Sing a growing set of songs
activities.goal: Singing in tune, memory for words and melody, and enjoyment.
activities.do: Sing together every day: in the car, at clean-up, at bedtime. Add a new song every week or two and keep the old ones in rotation.
activities.easier: Sing the last word of each line and let the child fill it in.
activities.harder: The child starts the song alone; sing a round or a call-and-response; make up a new verse.
activities.materials: None.
activities.why: Singing accuracy improves through the elementary years, and adults who stop singing sing about as accurately as kindergartners (`demorest-2015`); children without music instruction declined in singing over a year (`ilari-2016`). Shared home music at 2-3 had small associations with later skills (`williams-2015`). Correlational and cross-sectional evidence.
activities.notice: Is the child matching the tune or chanting the words?

activities.title: Sing back a note, then a tune
activities.goal: Hearing a pitch and matching it with the voice.
activities.do: Sing one note on a syllable ("la") and have the child sing it back. Then a slide up, a slide down, then a three-note pattern. Swap roles so the child leads. Use a keyboard note if your own voice wanders.
activities.easier: Match a sound in their own comfortable range; use a siren slide rather than a fixed note.
activities.harder: Five-note patterns; echo the first line of a song; find the note on a keyboard.
activities.materials: Voice; optionally a keyboard or a tuner app.
activities.why: No study tests this exact game. Singing accuracy is a skill that improves with use and declines without it (`demorest-2015`).
activities.notice: Does the child land on the note, or near it? Is it better on slides than fixed notes?

activities.title: Make music together as a family
activities.goal: Coordinating with other people in time.
activities.do: Play, sing or dance together as a group, with siblings included. Take turns leading: the leader sets the beat or the move and everyone follows.
activities.easier: Free dancing to a favourite song.
activities.harder: Start and stop together on a signal; play loud and soft together; each person keeps a different part.
activities.materials: Shakers, drums, pots, voices.
activities.why: Four-year-olds helped and cooperated more straight after making music together than after a matched non-musical game (`kirschner-2010`), and a school year of musical group games raised older children's empathy (`rabinowitch-2013`). Short-term lab effects and a small study; durable effects are unproven.
activities.notice: Can the child follow another person's lead as well as lead?

activities.title: Join a group music class
activities.goal: Making music with other children and a teacher, outside the family.
activities.do: Enrol in a weekly group class for this age: a children's band, choir, rhythm or general music class. Ask what the class does at home between sessions and do some of it.
activities.easier: A parent-and-child class.
activities.harder: A class with performances; a class built around one instrument.
activities.materials: A local music school or community class.
activities.why: Preschoolers had lower stress hormone after music, dance and art classes than after ordinary classes (`brown-2017`). Brief preschool music classes did not raise spatial, language or number skills (`mehr-2013`), so choose a class for the music and the enjoyment.
activities.notice: Does the child sing or play what they learned at home, unprompted?

activities.title: Listen to something new each week
activities.goal: Breadth: hearing many kinds of music and naming what is in it.
activities.do: Each week, put on one piece from a style or tradition the child has not heard: a symphony movement, jazz, a West African drum ensemble, a sitar raga, bluegrass. Name one instrument to listen for. Ask whether it sounds happy, sad, fast, slow, and why.
activities.easier: Two minutes, with movement allowed.
activities.harder: Pick out two instruments; compare two pieces; draw what the music sounds like; choose next week's piece from two options.
activities.materials: A streaming service or library recordings.
activities.why: No study tests wide listening at this age. It supplies the new triggers that early interest depends on (`hidi-renninger-2006`).
activities.notice: Which pieces does the child ask to hear again?

activities.title: Dance and freeze to music
activities.goal: Moving in time, and stopping and starting on a musical cue.
activities.do: Play music and dance freely; when the music stops, everyone freezes. Then dance fast for fast music and slow for slow, big for loud and small for quiet.
activities.easier: Free dancing only.
activities.harder: Freeze in a named shape or animal; move only when a particular instrument plays.
activities.materials: Any music and some space.
activities.why: A small trial of a creative dance program found no significant gain in social competence (`lobo-2006`). Do it for the movement and the musical listening.
activities.notice: Does the child react to changes in the music, or only to it stopping?
activities.safety: Clear the floor of trip hazards.

activities.title: Hear live music
activities.goal: Seeing and hearing instruments played by people in front of them.
activities.do: Every month or two, go to a free children's concert, an outdoor concert, a church or school performance, or a busker. Sit close enough to see the instruments. Afterwards, ask which instrument they liked and why.
activities.easier: Ten minutes of an outdoor concert.
activities.harder: Learn the name and family of each instrument; meet a musician and ask a question.
activities.materials: Library, park, school and orchestra family concerts.
activities.why: No study tests concerts at this age. A live theatre trial with older students (`greene-2017`) suggests live performance can do things a recording does not.
activities.notice: Which instrument does the child talk about afterwards?
activities.safety: Use ear protection for loud venues.

activities.title: Explore a real instrument
activities.goal: Finding out how an instrument makes high, low, loud and soft sounds.
activities.do: Give the child regular free access to a real instrument such as a keyboard, ukulele or xylophone. Show how to make a sound, then let them explore. Pick out a tune they know by ear together.
activities.easier: Find the highest and the lowest sound.
activities.harder: Play a three-note tune from memory; copy a short phrase you play.
activities.materials: Keyboard, ukulele, xylophone or recorder.
activities.why: Children's brains adapt to the instrument skill they practise (`hyde-2009`), but piano lessons did not leave a lasting advantage in other abilities (`costa-giomi-1999`). Do it to learn the instrument.
activities.notice: Does the child return to the instrument unprompted?

activities.title: Decide on formal lessons
activities.goal: Starting individual instrument lessons at a point where they are likely to stick.
activities.do: Wait for signs: the child asks repeatedly, returns to an instrument unprompted, and can attend for 15 minutes. Then book a short trial term with a teacher who teaches young children. At home, practise little and often, and focus on how: slow down the hard bar, play it three times right, then put it back in the piece.
activities.easier: Keep exploring and group class; revisit in three months.
activities.harder: A full term with a small performance at the end; the child keeps a practice chart.
activities.materials: A teacher and an instrument sized for the child.
activities.cadence: practice 4-5 days a week once started
activities.why: Practice explains about a fifth of differences in music performance (`macnamara-2014`), and how beginners practise predicts progress more than how long (`mcpherson-2005`). Whether lessons help other skills is contested (`sala-2020` against `roman-caballero-2022`); do not start them for that.
activities.notice: Does the child practise without reminders after the first month?

activities.title: Sample a new activity each season
activities.goal: Breadth: trying unfamiliar activities before settling on a few.
activities.do: Each season, sign up for one short taster of something the child has not done: a sport, a dance style, an art class, a music class, a nature program, chess, swimming. Commit to finishing the taster, then decide together whether to continue.
activities.easier: A single drop-in session.
activities.harder: The child chooses from a list of three; keep one activity going while sampling another.
activities.materials: Community centre, library and parks programs.
activities.why: World-class athletes did more varied sport in childhood and specialised later than national-level ones (`gullich-2022`), and organised activities go with better outcomes while true over-scheduling is rare (`mahoney-2006`). Both are correlational and about older children.
activities.notice: Which activities does the child ask to go back to? Which do they want to stop, and why?
activities.safety: Check coach and instructor safety practices.

activities.title: Go deep on a passion
activities.goal: Turning an intense interest into knowledge, questions and skills.
activities.do: When the child is fixated on a topic (dinosaurs, trucks, space, sharks), feed it: library nonfiction, a museum, a documentary, an expert to ask. Then use it as a doorway: count the dinosaurs, draw them, sort them by period, write labels, build a model.
activities.easier: One book and one conversation.
activities.harder: The child asks a question you cannot answer and you find out together; they make a book or a talk about it for the family.
activities.materials: Library, museums, the topic itself.
activities.why: Nearly a third of young children have an intense interest (`deloache-2007`), early science interests are sustained when families supply chances to learn (`alexander-2012`), and curiosity predicts kindergarten reading and math (`shah-2018`). Correlational evidence.
activities.notice: Does the child generate new questions, or just repeat known facts?
